body_text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part II (Evaluation of Integrals).
Let $f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be Riemann integrable. If $G : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$
is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$ with $G'(x) = f(x)$
(that is, $G$ is an antiderivative of $f$), then:
$$ \int_a^b f(x) \, dx = G(b) - G(a). $$

*Proof*: Let $P = \{a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b\}$ be any partition of $[a, b]$.
By the Mean Value Theorem applied to $G$ on each subinterval $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$,
there exists $t_i \in (x_{i-1}, x_i)$ such that:
$$ G(x_i) - G(x_{i-1}) = G'(t_i)(x_i - x_{i-1}) = f(t_i) \Delta x_i. $$
Summing these differences telescopically:
$$ G(b) - G(a) = \sum_{i=1}^n (G(x_i) - G(x_{i-1})) = \sum_{i=1}^n f(t_i) \Delta x_i. $$
Since $m_i \leq f(t_i) \leq M_i$, this Riemann sum is bounded by $L(f, P) \leq G(b) - G(a) \leq U(f, P)$.
Since $f$ is Riemann integrable, taking the limit as mesh $\|P\| \to 0$ forces
$G(b) - G(a) = \int_a^b f(x) \, dx$.
